title: Our method in each style
teaches: The same steps run every trade, day, swing or position: find the setup, set the stop, size from it, manage it, review it, under our 2% ceiling. What changes with the clock is the chart you read, where the stop sits and so the size, and whether you carry gaps overnight.

facts.quote: If the market’s moving fast, you could receive less—and potentially significantly less—than $50 per share by the time your order is executed.
facts.claim: In a fast market, a triggered sell stop can fill well below the stop price.

facts.quote: Rapid price movement during a short period of time could trigger a stop order. Due to market volatility, the stock might later rebound and resume trading at its prior price level.
facts.claim: A quick drop can trigger a stop, and the stock can then bounce right back.

facts.quote: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order. The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: A stop price is a trigger for a market order, not a guaranteed fill price.

facts.quote: A stop order may be triggered by a short-term, intraday price move that results in an execution price for the stop order that is substantially worse than the stock’s closing price for the day.
facts.claim: A short intraday move can trigger a stop and fill it far below where the stock closes.

facts.quote: domestic issuers must submit annual reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, and current reports on
facts.claim: US public companies file an annual report (10-K) and quarterly reports (10-Q).

facts.quote: The report must be filed for each of the first three fiscal quarters of the company's fiscal year.
facts.claim: A 10-Q is filed for each of the first three quarters; the 10-K covers the year, so a report comes every quarter.

facts.quote: Unlike day traders, swing traders hold positions overnight but target shorter-term opportunities than position traders or long-term investors.
facts.claim: Swing traders hold overnight; day traders don't, and position traders hold longer.

facts.quote: Swing traders, on the other hand, hold their positions for days or weeks. This exposes them to the risk of potential gaps at the market open due to news that occurred during non-trading hours.
facts.claim: Holding for days or weeks exposes a swing trade to gaps at the open from news after hours.

facts.quote: Many swing traders also track market fundamentals, longer-term trends, and economic cycles to ensure they aren't trading against the broader market.
facts.claim: Swing traders watch the broader market so they aren't trading against it.

facts.quote: A position trader would likely weather these shifts as long as the trend remains intact, while a swing trader might target multiple trading opportunities within the longer move.
facts.claim: A position trader sits through the pullbacks while the trend holds; a swing trader trades the smaller swings inside it.

facts.quote: In addition to a solid trading plan—including when to enter and exit trades, how much capital to risk on each position, and which securities to trade—day traders rely on a variety of tools
facts.claim: A day trader's plan still sets when to enter and exit, how much to risk and what to trade.

facts.quote: The key is that every position is opened and closed on the same day.
facts.claim: A day trade is opened and closed on the same day.

facts.quote: But this can also lead to bigger losses. A small price move in the wrong direction can wipe out a significant portion of your account.
facts.claim: With borrowed money, a small move against you can wipe out a big part of the account.

facts.quote: A trade boils down to a series of decisions about what to trade, how much to trade, when to enter, and when to exit.
facts.claim: Every trade is the same set of decisions: what, how much, when in, when out.

facts.quote: Closing out the trade isn't the final step; instead, you need to evaluate your results.
facts.claim: After you close a trade, you still review how it went.

facts.quote: Record your trades in a trading journal.
facts.claim: Keep a journal of your trades.

facts.quote: For a general rule, some traders may risk up to 1%–2% of their account on a single trade and allocate up to 5%–10% of their portfolio in any single position.
facts.claim: Risk per trade and position size are two separate limits.

facts.quote: Start with the difference between the entry price, $67, and the exit price, $57, or $10, then divide the amount the trader is willing to lose, $750, by that difference to determine the number of shares
facts.claim: Shares are the dollars you'll risk divided by the distance from entry to stop.

facts.quote: Some traders consider placing a stop under the lowest price reached in the first 10 minutes.
facts.claim: A stop some traders use on a trade near the open: under the low of the first 10 minutes.

facts.quote: Conversely, a longer-term trader may choose to evaluate exit strategies over a longer timeframe, rather than worrying about intraday or short-term levels of potential support. As always, traders must know their timeframe for every trade.
facts.claim: A longer-term trader judges exits on a longer timeframe, not intraday levels; know your timeframe for every trade.

facts.quote: You never know what news might hit after the close, and there's always the potential for the stock to gap lower the next trading day.
facts.claim: News after the close can gap a stock lower the next day.

facts.quote: Deciding which SMA time frame to use often comes down to the trading time horizon.
facts.claim: The moving average you use should fit how long you hold.

facts.quote: If a trader rarely holds a stock for more than 10 trading days, for example, the 20- or even 10-day SMA may provide good insights into how a stock's price has been moving recently.
facts.claim: For holds of about 10 trading days or less, the 10 or 20-day average fits.

facts.quote: If someone is more of a "position" trader—that is, they're willing to hold a stock for up to a year—the 200-day SMA is going to give a better sense of a stock's long-term price pattern.
facts.claim: For a position trader holding up to a year, the 200-day average fits better.

facts.quote: Stop orders are vulnerable to pricing gaps, which can sometimes occur between trading sessions or during pauses in trading, such as trading halts.
facts.claim: A gap between sessions can carry the price past a stop.

facts.quote: If the stock gaps up or down on market open, the trade is likely to execute above or below the intended price, which can result in greater losses than expected.
facts.claim: A gap at the open can fill a stop away from its price and cost more than planned.

facts.quote: When the investor's economic and market outlook is strongly bearish (or turns negative), a more defensive posture could be instituted by limiting new buys, selling losers faster, tightening up stops and/or implementing some downside protection.
facts.claim: When the market outlook turns negative, buy less, sell losers faster and tighten stops.

facts.quote: A big factor in increasing the returns of your stock portfolio and preserving your capital may be going against your natural instincts by cutting your losses fast and letting your winners ride.
facts.claim: Cut losses fast and let winners ride.

facts.quote: instead of admitting we were wrong, cutting bait and moving on to our next idea. In fact, this can be one of the fastest ways to lose money in the stock market.
facts.claim: Buying more of a falling stock instead of admitting you were wrong is one of the fastest ways to lose money.

facts.quote: In my opinion, no one position should maintain such a large percentage that it determines the future of the portfolio.
facts.claim: No single position should be big enough to decide the whole account.

facts.quote: The 2% Rule. Not allowing a position to lose more than 2% of the overall portfolio.
facts.claim: Hirsch never lets one position lose more than 2% of the portfolio.

facts.quote: Use no more than a 20% stop loss on each position.
facts.claim: Hirsch, holding for the longer term, still caps each stop at 20%.

facts.quote: The important point is to develop a method that works for you; implement it consistently; adhere to explicit money management rules; and keep good records so you can track your progress as a trader.
facts.claim: Whatever the method: follow it, keep money rules, and keep records to track your progress.

facts.quote: Position traders may hold their position for many months or years.
facts.claim: A position trade can run for many months or years.

facts.quote: they hope that prices will rise through the periodic downturns that may frustrate traders with shorter investment time horizons.
facts.claim: Position traders hold through pullbacks that frustrate shorter-term traders.

facts.quote: what happens if the stock moves significantly over night? It was trading at 96 dollars the night before and
facts.claim: Fidelity's example: the stock was trading at 96 the night before.

facts.quote: You then sell at the next available price -- is closer to 90 bucks a share.
facts.claim: After an overnight earnings gap, the stop sold near 90.

facts.quote: In this particular example I mentioned this is called gapping risk where it could gap down and you're not guaranteed to get out at the 95
facts.claim: Gap risk: the stop was at 95, and a gap down meant no fill at 95.

facts.quote: This is a great order type for maybe a longer term trader. That they're trading a trend they see in the security. And maybe they want to trail by 10 percent
facts.claim: A longer-term trader riding a trend might trail a stop 10% below the high.

facts.quote: Success can require dedication, discipline, and strict money management controls.
facts.claim: Intraday trading needs strict money management, like any style.

facts.quote: The length of the moving average depends on the trader's time horizon and analytical objectives. Shorter moving averages (5-20 periods) are suitable for short-term trends and trading. Medium-term trends can be analyzed using longer moving averages (20-60 periods).
facts.claim: The average's length should match the time horizon: 5 to 20 periods short term, 20 to 60 medium term.

facts.quote: Long-term investors often use moving averages with 100 or more periods.
facts.claim: Long-term holders use averages of 100 periods or more.

facts.quote: A 10-day moving average will hug prices quite closely and turn shortly after prices turn.
facts.claim: A 10-day average hugs price and turns quickly.

facts.quote: Identify the setup Determine where your trade thesis fails (this is where you place your stop-loss) Measure the distance to invalidation Size your position LAST
facts.claim: The order: find the setup, put the stop where the idea fails, measure the distance, size last.

facts.quote: The biggest mistake is to decide on your position size first without calculating the space between entry and stop.
facts.claim: Picking a size before measuring entry to stop is the biggest sizing mistake.

facts.quote: In either case, place your stops where you think they’ll work. Just adjust your position.
facts.claim: Put the stop where it belongs and change the size instead.

facts.quote: Every trader—no matter your experience—needs a plan.
facts.claim: Every trader needs a written plan.

facts.quote: and you will thank yourself later. Objective Methodology Risk Management Trading Strategies Trader Log
facts.claim: CME lists a trader log among the five parts of a solid trading plan.

facts.quote: returns its own trigger (the entry) and stop for the candle it fires on.
facts.claim: Each of our setups comes with its own entry and stop.

facts.quote: The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: Our first trim, the hard rule: a third of the position at 3R. In practice the owner often waits for 5R.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: After the first third at 3R, we sell another third at 5R and trail the last third.

facts.claim: Our Kicker stop: under the Kicker's low, or 3.5% under entry if that is closer.

facts.claim: Our Kicker trail: under each higher low, or under the 10-day average.

facts.quote: It is an intraday entry in a stock that has already shown it can move.
facts.claim: The Go Signal is an intraday entry.

facts.quote: On the daily chart it fires when all of these hold:
facts.claim: The Go Signal is found on the daily chart.

facts.quote: Entry: the prior close when it traded that session (red to green), else the close. Stop: the session's low.
facts.claim: Go Signal plan: buy the prior close when it trades that session (else the close); stop at the session's low.

facts.quote: The real trigger is on the 30 or 65-minute chart, which the daily bar cannot see.
facts.claim: The Go Signal's real trigger is on the 30 or 65-minute chart.

facts.quote: 0.25% to 2% of the account, chosen by setup quality, your recent performance, market conditions and your edge. 2% is the hard ceiling.
facts.claim: Our risk per trade is 0.25% to 2% of the account, chosen by the setup, your results, the market and your edge; never above 2%.

facts.claim: Our default stop is the low of the day or the prior day's low.

facts.claim: Our rule: sell partials into strength and trail the rising moving averages.

walkthroughs.title: Same steps, any clock
steps: Every trade runs the same steps. Find the setup, set the stop, size from it, manage it, review it.
A day trade opens and closes the same day. A position trade can run for months.
What changes is the chart you read, where the stop sits, and so the size.

walkthroughs.title: What our rules set
steps: Our risk on any trade is 0.25% to 2% of the account. 2% is the hard ceiling.
Our default stop is the low of the day, or the prior day's low.
Each setup plan has its own stop. Our trims, a third at 3R and at 5R, are measured from it.

walkthroughs.title: What changes with the clock
steps: A short-term trader buying near the open might put the stop under the low of the first 10 minutes.
A longer-term trader judges exits on a longer timeframe, so the stop sits farther away.
Same risk, wider stop, smaller position. The size moves; the risk doesn't.

questions.q: You move from swing trades to day trades. Which part of your trade plan can you drop?
choices: None of it: same parts, less time
The stop, since you'll be watching
The size, it's only for a few hours
The exit, you're out by the close
questions.answer: None of it: same parts, less time
questions.why: None of it. Schwab's day-trading page lists the same plan parts: when to enter and exit, how much to risk, what to trade. Only the clock is shorter.
questions.lesson_line: A shorter hold is no reason for a thinner plan.

wrong.The stop, since you'll be watching: Watching isn't a stop. A fast drop can run through your price before you act, so the exit is set before you enter.
wrong.The size, it's only for a few hours: A few hours is plenty of time to lose. With borrowed money, a small move the wrong way can wipe out a big part of the account.
wrong.The exit, you're out by the close: The close is a deadline, not an exit plan. You still need the price that says you're wrong.

questions.q: Our 2% ceiling on risk per trade can stretch on a day trade, since you're out by the close.
questions.why: False. 2% is the hard ceiling on every trade. Our risk is chosen by setup quality, your recent results, market conditions and your edge. How long you hold isn't on that list. Being out by the close doesn't cap the loss either: a fast market can fill a stop well below it.
questions.lesson_line: One ceiling for every style: 2% of the account per trade.

questions.q: Day trade or position trade, what order do the steps go in?
questions.why: Setup, stop, size, manage, review. The stop goes where the idea fails, and the size comes from that distance. Closing the trade isn't the last step; reviewing it is.
questions.lesson_line: The order never changes. Only the clock does.

wrong.Setup, size, stop, manage, review: Size before stop is the mistake StockCharts calls the biggest. The distance to the stop is what sets the size.
wrong.Size, setup, stop, manage, review: A size picked before there's even a setup leaves the stop to be bent around it.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits.
questions.sentence: Same stock, same risk, wider stop: the position gets ___.
questions.why: Smaller. Shares are the dollars you'll risk divided by the distance to the stop. Move the stop farther away and the same risk buys fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: The chart sets the stop. The stop sets the size.

questions.q: On our plan, two trades with the same entry and stop get the same 3R trim, even if one is held longer.
questions.why: True. Our first trim is a third at 3R, measured from the stop. Same entry, same stop, same trim price, however long you hold.
questions.lesson_line: Trims are measured from the stop, not from the calendar.

questions.q: You time our Go Signal entry on the 30-minute chart. Where does the stop go?
questions.why: The session's low. Timing the entry intraday doesn't move the stop onto that clock. The Go Signal plan buys the prior close when it trades, and stops at the session's low.
questions.lesson_line: An intraday entry can still carry a daily stop. The Go Signal's is the low of the day.

wrong.Under the last 30-minute bar: That puts the stop on the entry's clock. The plan's stop is the session's low.
wrong.A flat 10% under entry: A flat percent ignores the chart. The plan names a real level: the session's low.
wrong.Just under the prior close: That's the entry level, so it leaves almost no room. The plan's stop is the session's low.

questions.q: A day trader dodges overnight gaps, so a day trade's stop fills right at the stop price.
questions.why: False. A triggered stop becomes a market order. In a fast market inside the day, the fill can be well below the stop price.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger, not a guaranteed price, in every style.

questions.q: You trade more than one style. Which of these changes from style to style?
questions.why: Where your stop sits. A short-term trader might use the low of the first 10 minutes. A longer-term trader judges exits on a longer timeframe. The ceiling, the plan and the review stay put.
questions.lesson_line: Know your timeframe for every trade. It decides where the stop goes.

wrong.Our 2% risk ceiling: That one never moves. 2% is our hard ceiling on any trade.
wrong.Having a written plan: Every style needs one. A day trader's plan sets the same things: when in, when out, how much to risk.
wrong.Reviewing your trades: Every style ends with a review. Closing the trade isn't the final step.

questions.q: A day trade: entry $18.60, stop $18.35, just under the first 10-minute low. You'll risk $200. How many shares?
questions.why: 800 shares. $200 divided by the distance from entry to stop. It's the same formula as a swing trade, with a tighter stop.
questions.lesson_line: Day trade or swing trade: shares are dollars at risk over risk per share.

questions.q: Several of our setup plans trail under the 10-day or 21-day average. Which of these three gives the best read on a hold of up to a year?
questions.why: The 200-day. The average should fit the hold. Schwab says a position trader willing to hold up to a year gets a better read from the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Same rule, longer clock: the average you watch should fit how long you hold.

wrong.The 10-day average: Schwab ties the 10 and 20-day to holds of 10 trading days or less. It hugs price and turns quickly, too fast for a hold of up to a year.
wrong.The 21-day average: ChartSchool puts 20 to 60 periods with medium-term trends. A hold of up to a year calls for a longer one.

questions.q: A Go Signal: you buy at $40.00, the prior close, with the stop at the session low of $39.20. Where is our first trim, 3R?
questions.why: $42.40. Our first trim is a third at 3R: three times the distance from your entry down to the session low, added to $40.00.
questions.lesson_line: 3R is three times your risk per share, added to the entry.

questions.story: You plan a position trade in a US company's stock. You expect to hold it for about six months.
questions.q: What must this plan cover that a day trade plan can skip?
choices: What you'll do at each quarterly report
Which hourly bar to buy on
Nothing extra, the stop covers it
questions.answer: What you'll do at each quarterly report
questions.why: What you'll do at each quarterly report. A US company files a report every quarter, and a hold that long spans more than one quarter. News outside trading hours can gap a stock past your stop by the next open.
questions.lesson_line: A long hold sits through quarterly reports. Decide what you'll do at each one before you buy.

wrong.Where the first 10-minute low is: That's a short-term stop for a trade near the open. A months-long hold judges exits on a longer timeframe.
wrong.Which hourly bar to buy on: Entry timing matters in both, but it does nothing for you when a report gaps the stock overnight.
wrong.Nothing extra, the stop covers it: A stop can't catch a gap. In Fidelity's example a stop at 95 sold near 90 after an overnight earnings report.

questions.q: A position trader who makes only a few trades a year can skip reviewing them.
questions.why: False. Closing out a trade isn't the final step; evaluating it is. Whatever the method, keep good records so you can track your progress.
questions.lesson_line: Every style ends the same way: log the trade and review it.

questions.story: You hold two swing trades and have new buys planned this week. Then the general market turns weak, and most stocks are falling.
questions.q: What's the right move?
choices: Ignore it, the stock is what counts
Widen your stops to ride it out
Buy more, prices are lower now
questions.why: Fewer new buys, and tighter stops. Market conditions are one of the things our risk is chosen by. When the outlook turns bearish, Hirsch's answer is to limit new buys and tighten stops.
questions.lesson_line: When the general market turns weak, buy less and tighten up. Don't trade against it.

wrong.Ignore it, the stock is what counts: Swing traders track the broader market so they aren't trading against it. A falling market is the one to respect.
wrong.Widen your stops to ride it out: That adds risk just as the market turns against you. Hirsch's answer in a bearish turn is tighter stops.
wrong.Buy more, prices are lower now: Hirsch warns that buying more of a falling stock can be one of the fastest ways to lose money.

questions.q: Jeffrey Hirsch allows stops up to 20%, but no position may lose over 2% of the portfolio. With a 20% stop, how big can the position be?
questions.why: 10% of the portfolio. The 2% loss cap divided by the 20% stop. A wide long-term stop fits the 2% cap because the position is sized down to match.
questions.lesson_line: A wide stop on a long hold is fine. The size shrinks so the risk doesn't grow.

questions.story: Your day trade is up 2R at 3:45 p.m. and closing strong. You sized it for a tight intraday stop. No earnings are due, and you'd like to hold it a few days.
questions.q: If you hold it overnight, what has to change?
choices: Re-plan it: daily stop, size to fit
Keep the size, stop to breakeven
Keep the intraday stop and size
questions.answer: Re-plan it: daily stop, size to fit
questions.why: Re-plan it. For a hold of days, I'd use our default stop: the day's low or the prior day's low. A wider stop means a smaller size for the same risk, which can mean selling part of it into strength.
questions.lesson_line: Change the clock and you re-run the steps: new stop, new size.

wrong.Nothing, it's already working: The plan was built for one day. News after the close can gap it, and the stop was set for intraday moves.
wrong.Keep the size, stop to breakeven: A breakeven stop can't catch an overnight gap, and the size was built for a tight intraday stop. A gap down at that size costs far more than planned.
wrong.Keep the intraday stop and size: A tight intraday stop sits inside a normal day's swings, so a hold of days can get stopped out early. It can't catch an overnight gap either.

questions.story: Two traders own the same stock. It pulls back to its 50-day average, and the long uptrend is intact. The swing trader's stop is hit. The position trader's stop sits lower and isn't touched.
questions.q: Who broke their plan?
questions.why: Neither. A position trader sits through pullbacks while the trend holds. A swing trader trades the smaller swings inside it. Each stop sits on its own timeframe.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out on one clock can be noise on a longer one. Judge each trade by its own plan.

wrong.The position trader, for holding: That stop sits on a longer timeframe, and this pullback didn't reach it. Holding is the plan.
wrong.The swing trader, for selling: Taking the stop was the plan. Holding past it would have been the mistake.
wrong.Both, the stops should match: Different holds need different stops. Matching them would put one trader on the wrong clock.

questions.story: You buy our Kicker at $50.00. The Kicker candle's low is $47.00.
questions.q: Where does our stop go?
questions.why: $48.25. Our Kicker stop is under the Kicker's low, or 3.5% under the entry if that's closer. 3.5% under $50.00 is closer than $47.00.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker stop: under the Kicker's low, or 3.5% under entry, whichever is closer.

wrong.Just under $47.00, the candle's low: That's the other half of the rule. 3.5% under entry is closer here, so it wins.
wrong.$45.00, 10% under entry: A flat 10% isn't in the Kicker plan. The rule is the candle's low or 3.5%, whichever is closer.

questions.story: Your day trades put 25% of the account in, with stops 2% under entry. You switch to position trades, keep 25% positions, and set stops 10% under.
questions.q: What's the problem?
choices: Risk is now 2.5%, over our ceiling
Risk fell, the stop is farther away
questions.answer: Risk is now 2.5%, over our ceiling
questions.why: Risk is now 2.5%, over our ceiling. Risk is size times stop distance: 25% times 10%. The stop went from 2% to 10% and the size didn't move.
questions.lesson_line: Switch to wider stops and the size must shrink. Never carry your old size onto a new clock.

wrong.None, the size didn't change: The size is the problem. Risk is size times stop distance, and the stop went from 2% to 10%.
wrong.Risk fell, the stop is farther away: A farther stop means more loss per share. With the same size, the risk goes up, not down.
wrong.Risk is still 0.5% a trade: That was your day-trade risk: 25% times 2%. The new stop changes the math.

questions.story: A day trade. Your stop is 0.25% under entry, at the low of the first few minutes. You risk 1% of the account, as on your swing trades.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Buy a capped size, far under 400%
Widen the stop to shrink the size
questions.answer: Buy a capped size, far under 400%
questions.why: Buy a capped size. 1% risk over a 0.25% stop works out to 400% of the account. Risk per trade and position size are two separate limits.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop doesn't license a giant position. Cap the size.

wrong.Buy the full 400%, on margin: With borrowed money, a small move against you can wipe out a big part of the account. And a fast market can fill a stop well below it.
wrong.Widen the stop to shrink the size: The stop belongs where the idea fails. Moving it to fix the size gets it backwards; adjust the position instead.
wrong.Tighten the stop even more: A tighter stop makes the formula's size even bigger, and normal swings hit it sooner.
